items.heading: Say "I Want a Safe
items.text: Say "I Want a Safe Say "I Want a Safe Say "I want a safe career" to five different people and you will get five different translations. A mother hears "won't put you in danger." A father hears "won't need a loan we cannot repay." A recruiter hears "low risk of you quitting." You might mean all three, plus a fourth thing nobody said out loud: will this job still respect me the same way in year six.

items.heading: The Entry the Entry
items.text: The Entry The entry-door trap. IT looks safe because entry-level hiring of women is genuinely strong - nearly a third of the workforce. The safety quietly disappears higher up: women hold only about 13-23% of senior tech and leadership roles depending on the study. A field can be safe to enter and unsafe to advance in at the same time.

rows: Any workplace with 10+ employees must have an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC). Complaints must be resolved within 90 days, extendable once.
A 2023 ILO review found most Indian employers still have not implemented this properly - ask about the ICC directly in any interview, do not assume it exists.
26 weeks of paid maternity leave for the first two children, creche mandate for establishments with 50+ employees.
Enforcement is strongest in large organised-sector employers - government, PSU banks, large IT and pharma companies. Small firms and gig-style roles often route around it entirely.

items.heading: The "Safe Field" Ceiling
items.text: The "safe field" ceiling. Teaching and nursing are steered toward women partly because they are seen as "suitable" - and partly because keeping wages modest in female-heavy fields is easier when the field is treated as secondary income, not primary. Research on occupational segregation calls this exact pattern out directly: it is not that these fields lack value, it is that the perception of "safe" gets used to justify a lower ceiling.

items.heading: The Flexibility Penalty
items.text: The flexibility penalty. Remote and work-from-home roles get marketed as the "safest" option because they remove the commute risk entirely. But recent reporting on India's hybrid workforce shows companies quietly promoting the people who show up in person over those who work remotely - so the safety of avoiding a commute can come with a real cost to promotion speed.

items.heading: The Mid
items.text: The mid-career cliff. The sharpest drop in women's workforce participation happens between 3 and 8 years of experience - not at entry, and not right before retirement. A field that looks completely safe in year one can turn into the riskiest stretch of the whole career by year five, when career breaks and rigid hours collide.

items.heading: The One
items.text: The one-safety trap. A job can score high on family approval and income stability, and still fail on physical safety if the shift timing or transport was never actually checked. Chasing only one kind of safety, and assuming the others come free with it, is the single most common mistake in this decision.

items.heading: IT Repeats "Teaching, Nursing, Government
items.text: It repeats "teaching, nursing, government job" without explaining which specific safety each one is strong on and which it is weak on.

items.heading: IT Skips the Actual Laws
items.text: It skips the actual laws that protect you at work - so you cannot tell a genuinely protected employer from one that just sounds calm.

items.heading: IT Never Mentions That "Safe"
items.text: It never mentions that "safe" fields often carry a lower pay ceiling as a direct trade-off, not a coincidence.

items.heading: IT Treats Family Approval As
items.text: It treats family approval as the only safety that matters, when income and legal protection matter just as much for your actual life.
